title: V. V. Giri and the National Labour Institute that bears his name
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Who was V. V. Giri, and what does the institute named for him do?
body:
Every labour movement needs two things besides courage: leaders who understand workers' lives and institutions that can study those lives with care. This post looks at one of each. **Varahagiri Venkata Giri** was a trade union organiser who became Labour Minister and then President of India. The **V. V. Giri National Labour Institute** in Noida carries his name and does research and training on labour questions for the Government of India. Understanding both helps readers see how India's labour policy has been argued, studied and taught.

## The man: from railway union to Rashtrapati Bhavan

V. V. Giri was born on 10 August 1894 in Berhampur, then in the Madras Presidency, in what is now Brahmapur in Odisha. He died in Madras, now Chennai, on 24 June 1980, aged 85. He made his public name through the labour movement.

His union career is substantial. He was a founding member of the **All India Railwaymen's Federation**, formed in 1923, and served as its general secretary for over a decade. He was elected president of the **All India Trade Union Congress** in 1926 and again in 1942. In 1928 he led a non-violent strike of Bengal Nagpur Railway workers against retrenchment, which accounts of his life describe as a milestone for the Indian labour movement. In 1929, with N. M. Joshi, he helped form the Indian Trade Union Federation, which merged back into the AITUC in 1939.

## Minister and President

Giri held labour portfolios in government. He served as Minister of Labour in the Madras government in 1937 to 1939 and again in 1946 to 1947, and as Union Minister of Labour from 1952 until he resigned in 1954. He went on to become the fourth President of India. After serving as acting President from 3 May to 20 July 1969, he was elected and held the office of President from 24 August 1969 to 24 August 1974. He was awarded the **Bharat Ratna** in 1975.

## The Giri approach

Giri is remembered in labour policy for what is known as the **Giri approach** to industrial disputes. In essence, it favours settling disputes through negotiation between management and workers, and, if talks fail, through further negotiation with the help of conciliation officers, rather than sending every dispute straight to compulsory adjudication. The idea is that a settlement that both sides have shaped is more durable than an award imposed from above.

This thinking is relevant today. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 retains conciliation as the first stage of a dispute and sets time limits within which a worker can go on to a tribunal. Debates about how much to rely on bargaining and how much on adjudication are old, and Giri's approach is part of that history. Among his writings are a book on industrial relations and labour problems in Indian industry, and a memoir, *My Life and Times*, published in 1976.

## The institute

The **V. V. Giri National Labour Institute (VVGNLI)** is at Noida, in Uttar Pradesh. It is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, Government of India. It was established in 1974 as the National Labour Institute and was renamed in 1995 in honour of Giri, who had been an early union leader as well as a former President.

The institute has its own governance. The Union Minister for Labour and Employment presides over the General Council, and the Executive Council is chaired by the Union Labour and Employment Secretary. A Director General is the administrative head. The institute also has partnerships with universities and research bodies, including plans reported from 2019 to offer research degrees with Jawaharlal Nehru University.

## What it does

According to the institute's own website, "research occupies a primary place" in its activities, and its research centres look at labour markets, employment relations, child labour, gender, climate change and the North-East. Its work falls into a few broad areas:

- **Research** on labour, employment, social security and industrial relations, often used to inform policy.
- **Training** programmes, both in India and for international participants, for labour administrators, trade union leaders, public sector managers and other functionaries. The institute also holds seminars, workshops and lectures.
- **Publications**, including the journal *Awards Digest: Journal of Labour Legislation*, the newsletters *Shram Vidhan* and *Indradhanush*, an annual report, and research studies and policy perspectives.
- **A library and online resources** on the labour codes, Acts and rules.
- **Networking**, through memoranda of understanding with universities and research institutions.

## Why research matters to a union

A movement that argues from first principles, as BMS does, still needs data. When a union says that contract work is growing, that wages in a sector are too low, or that a scheme's coverage is thin, it is more persuasive when it can point to studies. Equally, when the Government proposes a rule, it helps to know what comparable evidence says. The institute's library, publications and training modules are useful to both sides of such a conversation.

Training programmes also matter. Many office-bearers learn the practical side of labour law, such as how conciliation works, how to read a wage register, or what an inspector can and cannot do, by attending courses. Trade union leaders from different organisations, including BMS, can take part in programmes offered at institutions like this one.

## BMS and the wider ecosystem

BMS was founded in 1955 by Dattopant Thengadi, who was born in 1920 and died in 2004. Giri and Thengadi came from different traditions and were active in different periods, yet both are part of the story of Indian labour. BMS has its own training and research efforts, and it also engages with Government institutions. Other bodies that serve a similar educational purpose are the Dattopant Thengadi National Board for Workers' Education and Development, which we cover in the next post.

## For readers

If you want to understand labour questions with evidence, the institute's website is a good place to begin. Look for its publications section for the journal and newsletters, its library page for the text of the labour codes, and its training calendar for programmes open to union leaders and officials. Always check the date of any study, since labour markets change quickly.
